subject: old rubber tyres pile
title: What If 92% of a Country's Rubber Vanished? In 1942, America's Did

scenes.text: What if 92 percent of your country's rubber vanished? In 1942, America's did.
Japan had seized the plantations of Southeast Asia. President Roosevelt went on the radio: 92 percent of the normal supply, cut off.
A heavy bomber needed about 1,800 pounds of rubber. A scout car, 300. A gas mask, over a pound. No rubber, no war.
So for two weeks in June 1942, every gas station bought scrap: old tyres, hoses, boots, at a penny a pound. Around 450,000 tons came in.
Gasoline was rationed partly to save tyres, and anyone with more than five tyres had to sell the extras back.
Then 51 synthetic rubber factories went up, contracted for 400,000 tons a year. By 1944, supply met demand, from factories, not trees.

description:
What if a country lost 92 percent of its rubber overnight? In 1942 the United States did, when Japan took the plantations of Southeast Asia.
In a radio address on 12 June 1942, President Roosevelt said 92 percent of the normal rubber supply had been cut off and launched a two-week scrap rubber drive, with filling stations paying a penny a pound; about 450,000 tons were collected. Gasoline rationing and limits of five tyres per car were used to stretch supplies, and 51 government-funded synthetic rubber plants were built, contracted for 400,000 tons a year; by 1944 supply met demand.
